infrastructure_from_code_paradigm.traditional_yaml_k8s: Helm charts + ConfigMaps + Helm releases + kubectl + docker push + image pull on each node; declarative but disconnected from application code; feedback loop minutes-to-hours
infrastructure_from_code_paradigm.modal_decorator: @app.function(image=modal.Image.debian_slim().pip_install('torch'), gpu='H100', memory=4096); python -m modal deploy app.py
infrastructure_from_code_paradigm.ceo_quote: We decided to not build this on top of tools like Docker/Kubernetes because we want infrastructure to be _fast_. ... Modal has no problem building a 100GB container, and then booting up 100 of those containers — you can do the whole thing in a few seconds.

runtime_and_virtualization.container_runtime: gVisor's runsc (the 'run Sandboxed Container' OCI runtime). Modal contributes upstream to gVisor — Modal engineer Jonathon Belotti has commits (e.g., 85d1e860166348b4ae71bc1067ccf2613938c29e on the nvproxy sub-component that brokers GPU kernel-driver access).
runtime_and_virtualization.why_not_docker_runc: runsc runs in user-space (Go-implemented kernel = 'Sentry'); syscall surface reduced; checkpoint/restore is implemented as serializing the runtime's async/await state machine; easier to checkpoint and restore than runc.
runtime_and_virtualization.alternative_runtime: VM Sandboxes (alpha, 2026-06-15) — KVM-backed real Linux kernel; required for Docker-in-Docker, eBPF, systemd, cgroups. Uses experimental_options={'vm_runtime': True}.
runtime_and_virtualization.isolation_industry_placement: Layer 2 (user-space kernel); weaker than Firecracker (KVM microVM) for hostile code, but Modal has run it at scale to 1M concurrent sandboxes. Third-party benchmarks put Modal cold start ~600ms vs Firecracker-based E2B ~180ms / Vercel ~250ms.

image_loading.design: Container image = small (~5 MiB) content-addressed index of file metadata; file contents fetched on-demand via HTTP range requests
image_loading.library: libfuse (Modal's filesystem is a FUSE server)
image_loading.mount_latency: ~2 ms once the index is loaded
image_loading.index_load_latency: 1–100 ms depending on cache tier (memory / SSD / AZ cache / regional CDN / blob)
image_loading.data_path: Python container process → FUSE server → host page cache → SSD → AZ cache server → regional CDN → blob (S3-style)
modal_critical_optimizations: Tuned read_ahead_kb from default 128 → 32 MiB on big hosts. 1 GiB caused 'disastrous latency issues in production' (per Belotti 2024).
FUSE request size lifted from 128 KiB to 1 MiB
Skip gzip decompression entirely: 'DEFLATE is inherently single-threaded (LZ77, Huffman) which limits you to ~100 MB/s'
zstd used where Modal controls the build; otherwise raw
Workers: AWS 8-GPU instances with ~5 GB/s down + RAID-0 SSD
Multi-flow download (multiple src IP/port/protocol) to dodge per-flow throttling
image_loading.measured_throughput: ~800 MB/s initial → ~2.5 GB/s after tuning (loads 512 MiB .safetensors in 200ms from disk cache, ~300ms from network)

cold_start_elimination.three_pillars: 1) Custom content-addressed filesystem (ImageFS); 2) CPU memory snapshot via CRIU + gVisor; 3) GPU memory snapshot via NVIDIA CUDA checkpoint API (drivers 570/575 branch)

cpu_snapshot.tech: CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) — originally a 'mad Russians' 2011 Linux kernel patch (commit 099469502f62fbe0d7e4f0b83a2f22538367f734). Implemented inside gVisor's Sentry (Go) — at least 18 components implement save_restore.go; serializes the cooperative-preemption state machine.
cpu_snapshot.snapshot_trigger: On-demand, not proactive. Per snapshot_info: Optional[api_pb2.SnapshotInfo] = await get_or_create_checkpoint_for_worker_and_task(...). A single Function version is snapshotted multiple times because snapshot must match the host (instruction set, OS micro-version).
cpu_snapshot.api: enable_memory_snapshot=True on @app.function; @modal.enter(snap=True) for setup hooks that should run before snapshot
cpu_snapshot.performance: Stable Diffusion: 13s normal → 3.5s restore (2.5x); import torch: ~5s normal → 1.05s p50 / 0.69s p0

gpu_snapshot.tech: NVIDIA CUDA checkpoint API (cuCheckpointProcessLock / cuCheckpointProcessRestore / cuCheckpointProcessUnlock); available in datacenter driver branches 570 / 575
gpu_snapshot.approach: Lock CUDA processes → wait for CU_PROCESS_STATE_CHECKPOINTED with no active sessions → snapshot CPU+GPU memory together → on restore, reverse: cuCheckpointProcessRestore then cuCheckpointProcessUnlock. Entirely integrated into the gVisor checkpoint/restore system; falls back to CPU-only snapshot if hardware mismatch.
gpu_snapshot.constraints: Multi-GPU programs with NCCL are fragile (deadlock on pause); vLLM / SGLang need weight offloading + recreation of empty KV cache
gpu_snapshot.performance: Parakeet (NeMo): 20s P0 → 2s P0 (10x); ViT+torch.compile: 8.5s P0 → 2.25s P0; vLLM Qwen2.5-0.5B: 45s P0 → 5s P0

cold_start_elimination.container_start_lifetime: Modal's docs state containers boot in ~1 second at the runsc layer; user code init time is what snapshot restore then attacks.
cold_start_elimination.heterogeneous_cloud_constraint: AWS g6.12xlarge lacks pclmulqdq instruction — can't accept snapshots created on hosts that have it. Modal's multi-cloud fleet therefore creates multiple snapshots per Function version.

gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.mig_support: Modal does NOT publish MIG-backed vGPU in its public docs. Modal's fleet uses full-physical GPUs in 8-GPU nodes. It is the consumer of NVIDIA driver features (CUDA checkpoint API) rather than a vGPU provider.
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.gpu_sharing_strategy: Full physical GPU per Function by default. Sandboxes/Notebooks can share the underlying GPU only if the user code is multi-process on one device. MIG is a Modal-side capability gap — Modal's blog 'gpu-glossary' describes MIG abstractly.
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.scheduler_architecture: New (2026-07) architecture replaces original Postgres-backed central scheduler with horizontally scaled scheduling servers; each scheduling server runs a fast load-balancing algorithm against in-memory cached worker state; workers publish state to a Redis stream (no central durable store on the critical path); two network hops + one cheap CPU op per sandbox create.
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.previous_architecture_pain_points: O(sandboxes) writes to un-shardable Postgres; central coordination bottleneck; heartbeats O(nodes)
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.1M_sandbox_benchmark: 1,000,000 sandboxes created concurrently in <60s; p50 time-to-interactivity <500ms; bottleneck is the benchmark client, not Modal
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.rtnl_lock_lesson: At scale, sandbox creation flooded the Linux kernel's rtnl lock (network rule setup) so heavily that container start took tens of seconds; Modal reworked container networking setup just to survive burst.
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.scaling_horizon: Single Redis stream viable to >100k workers; if needed, add more streams (no ordering required)
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.multi_cloud_capacity_orchestrator: 13+ cloud providers (per Erik Bernhardsson Reuters interview, up from 5 a year prior); the 'Resource Solver' is an LP (linear programming) wrapper around Google's GLOP solver (OR-Tools). Inputs: demand, cloud prices, capacity limits, GPU performance, region affinity; outputs: per-instance-type delta (spin-up/spin-down). Triggers cloud-provider instance API calls via background workers.
gpu_virtualization_and_scheduling.gpu_health_management: Weekly deep active checks (NVIDIA DCGM diag level 2, GPUBurn, NCCL all-reduce); four per-container GPU metrics (memory, utilization, temperature, power); Xid/sXid dictionary; targets ClusterMAX expectations.

volumes_v1_v2.v1: Distributed filesystem; 500k file soft limit; <5 concurrent writers recommended
volumes_v1_v2.v2: Hardlinks, unlimited files, concurrent writes from hundreds of containers, faster commit/reload, demand-loaded filesystem tree traversal (slower v2 listing but better write performance), HIPAA-compliant deletion (data destruction guaranteed on delete)

storage_and_distributed_io.design_intent: Write-once, read-many — exactly the shape of 'train model, push weights, read weights 1000x from inference replicas'
storage_and_distributed_io.implementation_hint: Modal does not publish the backing store. Best-inference from design docs: multi-cloud replication for availability; lazy fetch semantics consistent with ImageFS

module_4_blog_deconstruction.title: Fast, lazy container loading in Modal.com
module_4_blog_deconstruction.author: Jonathon Belotti
module_4_blog_deconstruction.problem_statement: Serverless cold start. Naive docker run of an 8 GiB 'fat Python' image takes ~1 minute (download at 2 GiB/s, single-thread gzip at 80 MiB/s, unpack onto rootfs). K8s tolerates this because pod churn is low; Modal's use case is hundreds of pods per minute.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.solution_details: ImageFS: container image becomes a ~5 MiB content-addressed index of file metadata; contents fetched on-demand via FUSE. Data path: Python container → FUSE server → host page cache → SSD → AZ cache server → regional CDN → blob. Read-ahead tuned from 128 KiB default to 32 MiB. FUSE request size from 128 KiB to 1 MiB. Skip gzip decompression entirely. RAID-0 SSD + multi-flow HTTP on 8-GPU AWS instances. Modal uses libfuse + Rust for the FUSE server.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.benchmarks: Initial 800 MB/s → current 2.5 GB/s. 512 MiB .safetensors loads in 200ms (disk cache) or 300ms (network). 1 GiB read-ahead caused 'disastrous latency issues in production' — Modal settled on 32 MB.

module_4_blog_deconstruction.title: Memory snapshots: Checkpoint/restore for sub-second startup
module_4_blog_deconstruction.author: Jonathon Belotti
module_4_blog_deconstruction.problem_statement: Even with a fast container, lazy image loading still has to pay the cost of executing the Python import system. import torch alone is 26,000 syscalls. Snapshot the process state after initialization and skip the imports on the next cold start.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.solution_details: Snapshots are CRIU-derived but adapted to gVisor's runsc. CRIU targets runc — Modal's runsc has 18+ save_restore.go components in its Sentry Go kernel. Snapshot = container's filesystem mutations + entire process tree (memory mappings, file descriptor table, registers, env vars, PID). Created on-demand, lazily, when scheduler doesn't have an existing snapshot for the target worker host. A single Function version may have multiple snapshots because instruction-set / OS differences between worker hosts prevent snapshot portability. Snapshot files stored as a single 'pages' file (100 MiB–10 GiB). gVisor's prioritized background page loading + Modal's FUSE-level aggressive preload cooperate to minimize aggregate page-fault latency.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.benchmarks: Stable Diffusion: 13s normal → 3.5s (2.5x). import torch: ~5s normal → 1.05s p50 / 0.69s p0. Restore is bound by 'main process memory mappings served into host page cache'.

module_4_blog_deconstruction.title: GPU Memory Snapshots: Supercharging sub-second startup
module_4_blog_deconstruction.author: Luis Capelo, Colin Weld
module_4_blog_deconstruction.problem_statement: CPU snapshots save a lot, but they don't include GPU state. So Model.to('cuda') had to run post-restore, eating the wins.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.solution_details: Integrate NVIDIA's CUDA checkpoint/restore API (driver branches 570 / 575). cuCheckpointProcessLock → wait for CU_PROCESS_STATE_CHECKPOINTED with no active CUDA sessions → snapshot CPU memory + GPU memory together → on restore, cuCheckpointProcessRestore then cuCheckpointProcessUnlock. Falls back to CPU-only snapshot on hardware mismatch. No longer need snap=True / snap=False lifecycle split.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.benchmarks: Parakeet (NeMo): 20s P0 → 2s P0 (10x). ViT+torch.compile: 8.5s → 2.25s. vLLM Qwen2.5-0.5B: 45s → 5s.

module_4_blog_deconstruction.title: How we achieved truly serverless GPUs
module_4_blog_deconstruction.author: Modal engineering team (cross-posted Erik)
module_4_blog_deconstruction.problem_statement: GPU allocation utilization for inference is often 10–20% because workloads are bursty and customers over-provision. The four bottlenecks to fix: (1) instance acquisition (minutes for GPU allocations); (2) machine management/boot; (3) container image + filesystem loading; (4) app-level host + device initialization. Naïve 2,000 s vs Modal 50 s for a fresh inference replica.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.solution_details: Four-ingredient architecture. (1) Multi-cloud capacity orchestrator (the Resource Solver) — 13+ cloud providers; LP via Google GLOP to choose where to spin up; min-cost arbitrages H200s < H100s periodically. (2) Cloud buffers — small idle GPU pool to absorb new load. (3) Custom filesystem (ImageFS) — lazy, content-addressed, multi-tier cache. (4) Checkpoint/restore for both CPU (CRIU+gVisor) and GPU (CUDA checkpoint API). The genuinely novel part: runsc's state-machine nature means CRIU-equivalent serialization is 'only a matter of serializing [the runtime's] state into a checkpoint'.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.benchmarks: 40x spin-up improvement (50s vs 2000s). vLLM Qwen3-0.6B boot: CPU+GPU snapshots reduce 95th-percentile restore time materially. g6.12xlarge (no pclmulqdq) cannot accept snapshots made on hosts that have it → heterogeneous fleet forces N snapshots per Function. RDMA weight server could lift model-load bandwidth 3–10x; not yet productized.

module_4_blog_deconstruction.title: Scaling to 1 million concurrent sandboxes in seconds
module_4_blog_deconstruction.author: Colin Weld, Connor Adams
module_4_blog_deconstruction.problem_statement: Run a million concurrent sandboxes (i.e., tens of thousands of nodes). Standard container schedulers (K8s) collapse: O(n·p) scheduling, serialized by default; every pod writes etcd; heartbeats are O(nodes); etcd is the write bottleneck and is not natively shardable within a keyspace. Modal's previous sandbox architecture had analogous Postgres problems — every create/schedule = Postgres write; durable workflow per finished sandbox = event backlog at high churn.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.solution_details: Throw out central coordination. (1) Fleet of scheduling servers handle create requests concurrently. (2) Each scheduler runs a load-balancing algorithm against in-memory cached worker state — looks more like LB than container scheduling. (3) Workers are themselves the source of truth; they publish state periodically to a Redis stream; schedulers consume async. (4) Scheduler picks a worker, RPCs it directly; worker accepts if it has free resources, else rejects. Only two network hops and one cheap CPU op on the create path. No central bottleneck. Also: redesigned container networking because rtnl lock contention made floods of sandbox creations take tens of seconds to set up.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.benchmarks: 1,000,000 sandboxes in <60 seconds. p50 time-to-interactivity <500 ms. Single Redis stream viable past 100,000 workers.

module_4_blog_deconstruction.title: Linear programming for fun and profit (Resource Solver)
module_4_blog_deconstruction.author: Colin Weld, Irfan Sharif
module_4_blog_deconstruction.problem_statement: Find optimal mix of cloud instance types to satisfy demand at minimum cost, given (a) per-instance price and capacity limits across 13+ providers; (b) demand variability; (c) buffer headroom for instant scale-up; (d) per-region mix constraints; (e) performance equivalence between GPU types.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.solution_details: Wrap Google's GLOP solver (OR-Tools). Formulate as LP. Pre-prune instance types heuristically (cut solve time by ~10x; lose a little accuracy). Solver emits a solution → background workers issue instance requests to providers → failures observed as scaling limits → fed back as constraints. 'Dual mandate' like the Fed: fast scaling and cost-optimality often conflict. Modal deliberately picked H200 over H100 when price/performance permitted, capturing arbitrage.
module_4_blog_deconstruction.benchmarks: Modal claims 'millions of dollars a year' saved via arbitrage. Recently captured hundreds of superior H200 GPUs at 20% discount to inferior H100s.

modal_architecture_tradeoffs: Vendor lock-in: Modal functions only run on Modal — no AWS / GCP / on-prem Modal. Cannot deploy 'Modal runtime' into customer VPC. (Daytona offers self-host; Modal deliberately does not.)
Edge customization constrained: regional routing exists but you cannot pin to a specific AZ, VPC, or on-prem rack

gVisor syscall coverage not perfect: some syscalls behave subtly differently vs. host kernel; certain kernel features (eBPF, raw sockets, Docker-in-Docker, custom cgroups, systemd) require the new alpha VM Sandboxes
Snapshot portability: snapshots are tied to host CPU instruction set + CUDA driver branch + GPU model. Heterogeneous fleet forces maintaining multiple snapshots per Function.
Pricing opacity: region multipliers 1.15–1.75x, non-preemptible 3x, Sandbox CPU 3x standard — making capacity planning harder
modal_architectural_advantages: Sub-1s GPU cold starts via stacking (ImageFS lazy load + CRIU CPU snapshot + CUDA checkpoint GPU snapshot)
Same Python DSL covers inference, batch, RL, sandboxes, training, notebooks — no infra-switching tax
Multi-cloud arbitrage via LP solver means Modal can offer competitive per-second prices even when no single provider is cheap
gVisor isolation + ephemeral-by-default sandboxes → safe to host hostile agent code
1M concurrent sandboxes proven; 50k concurrent per customer in production
modal_bottlenecks: InfiniBand/RoCE: Modal's own post explicitly notes a 3-10x bandwidth lift is possible with in-AZ RDMA weight servers, but 'expensive and gnarly, especially when scaling to many models and dynamic worker pools'. Not productized.
Multi-GPU training in production is closed beta; multi-node DDP is not first-class

GPU supply chain: Modal is itself a buyer of H100s/H200s/B200s from hyperscalers + Oracle + smaller clouds. CEO: 'we work with 13 cloud providers, up from 5 last year'. Vulnerable to upstream allocation.
Snapshot fallback: 100% restore success is not guaranteed; Modal falls back to cold start when CRIU/gVisor/CUDA APIs reject a snapshot, so worst-case latency still applies.

analyst_estimates.arr_progression: TechCrunch (2023-10) said monthly revenue 'six figures' (~$1M/year). Reuters (2026-05) reports Modal told them ARR was $60M in Sept 2025 and $300M in May 2026. Sacra corroborates $119M end-2025 → $300M April 2026. ARR likely to exit 2026 above $500M at the current 5x/8mo clip (modal.com Series C blog: 'surpassing $300 million in annualized revenue').
implied_gross_margin_logic: GPU cost @ $2-4/GPU-hr from cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Oracle, CoreWeave, Lambda) vs Modal's list $2.50-$6.25/GPU-hr (A100 80GB to B200).
Modal can sell at 30-100% gross markup on the cheapest H100 in steady-state.
But: idle buffer pool, fallback cold-starts, snapshot duplication across heterogeneous hosts, and three cloud-region multipliers (1.15x-1.75x) eat margin.
If Modal's true blended cost is ~$1.8/GPU-hr (LP arbitrage on H200, Oracle discount, spot) and average selling is ~$3.0/GPU-hr (mix of A100/H100/H200), gross margin is plausibly 35-50%.
For Inference serving only (not Sandboxes). Sandbox pricing is 3x standard CPU/memory, so gross margin on Sandbox is higher.
analyst_estimates.valuation_multiple: Series C $4.65B on $300M ARR = 15.5x forward revenue. Comparable to Fireworks (17.5x at Series D), Together (7x), Baseten (~21x).
analyst_estimates.implied_2027_exit_revenue: Linear extrapolation (5x in 8 months) would put Modal at $1.5B ARR by end-2026, $7.5B by end-2027 — clearly unsustainable. More realistic: 2-3x/year growth from a $300M base, implying ~$600-900M end-2026 and ~$1.5-2.5B end-2027.
